title: SCAI Cardiogenic Shock Staging
keywords: this stages severity within cardiogenic shock once diagnosed, it does not diagnose the mechanism, pair it with shock-classification for that
stage C is the classic cardiogenic shock most clinicians picture, but stages D and E are common ICU deterioration patterns that get missed if you re-anchor on the admission stage instead of restaging
roughly 1 percent mortality at stage A climbing to roughly 90 percent at stage E, this is one of the strongest mortality-predicting classifications in cardiac critical care
reassess the stage frequently, a patient can move from C to D to E within hours despite treatment
sources: Baran DA, et al. SCAI clinical expert consensus statement on the classification of cardiogenic shock. Catheter Cardiovasc Interv. 2019;94(1):29-37.
Jentzer JC, et al. Cardiogenic Shock Classification to Predict Mortality in the Cardiac Intensive Care Unit. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2019;74(17):2117-2128.

changelog.change: Initial entry — a genuine content gap (Content audit 2026-09-15, fresh-look Batch 7). The staging concept was already explained narratively inside shock-classification, but no dedicated staging tool existed, unlike other severity classifications in this app (Killip, APACHE-II). A classification, not a point score, so uses the classification engine type.

purpose: Stages cardiogenic shock severity from A (at risk) to E (extremis) — a strong, validated predictor of in-hospital mortality that also guides escalation urgency.
notes: Distinguish from SHOCK MECHANISM (see shock-classification) — this stages SEVERITY within cardiogenic shock specifically, once that diagnosis is established, and tracks closely with in-hospital mortality (roughly A <1%, B ~3%, C ~20%, D ~55%, E ~90% in the derivation cohort).

tiers.label: Stage A — At risk
tiers.description: No current signs/symptoms of cardiogenic shock, but at risk for its development (e.g. large anterior MI, prior decompensated heart failure).
tiers.mortality: Very low (approx. <1%) — close monitoring, no shock-specific intervention yet needed

tiers.label: Stage B — Beginning
tiers.description: Clinical evidence of relative hypotension or tachycardia WITHOUT hypoperfusion — normal or mildly elevated lactate (< 2 mmol/L).
tiers.mortality: Low (approx. 3%) — close monitoring, address the underlying cardiac process

tiers.label: Stage C — Classic
tiers.description: Hypoperfusion requiring intervention beyond volume resuscitation — meets hemodynamic criteria for cardiogenic shock (SBP <90 mmHg for >30 min, or need for pressors/inotropes/mechanical support to maintain SBP >90) WITH clinical congestion and lactate ≥2 but <5 mmol/L.
tiers.mortality: Substantial (approx. 20%) — pharmacologic support (pressors/inotropes), consider escalating monitoring/mechanical support evaluation

tiers.label: Stage D — Deteriorating
tiers.description: Similar to Stage C but FAILING to respond to initial interventions — lactate ≤5 mmol/L with end-organ dysfunction (renal/hepatic), OR lactate ≥5 mmol/L WITHOUT end-organ dysfunction, OR persistent hypoperfusion despite escalating support.
tiers.mortality: High (approx. 55%) — escalate support urgently, actively evaluate for mechanical circulatory support (IABP/Impella/VA-ECMO)

tiers.label: Stage E — Extremis
tiers.description: Cardiac arrest with ongoing CPR, and/or ECMO/mechanical circulatory support being emergently initiated, and/or refractory shock despite maximal support with multiple pressors/inotropes.
tiers.mortality: Very high (approx. 90%) — maximal resuscitative and mechanical circulatory support efforts

interpretation.label: Stage strongly predicts in-hospital and long-term mortality — reassess frequently, a patient can move between stages within hours
interpretation.detail: This is a severity/prognostic classification, not a treatment algorithm on its own — pair it with the mechanism-based workup in shock-classification and the device-selection considerations for escalating mechanical support.

buildNote: classification engine, matching the postpartum-hemorrhage-staging/killip-classification pattern. Stage criteria and approximate mortality figures WebSearch-verified against Baran et al. (2019 SCAI consensus statement) and Jentzer et al. (JACC 2019) — mortality figures presented as approximate since they vary somewhat across validation cohorts. Calculators carry no `related` field; cross-referenced to shock-classification and rv-failure-pulmonary-hypertensive-crisis via `notes` and keywords instead.
